CLASSROOM NOTEBOOK · FINAL REPORT

Saathi: a teacher copilot for India’s primary classrooms

Plan the lesson, check who learned, and know what to do next—with no student devices.

By Uday Addanki

GitHub repository
https://github.com/UdayAddanki/saathi

This repository is public. Graders can run it locally using the README and the demo account.

1. Motivation

I spent seven years in the education nonprofit sector in India, working closely with teachers and programme managers. Teachers are drained after a long school day and struggle to find time to prepare the next day's lessons, which hurts job satisfaction and contributes to teachers leaving. Primary classes have 35–50 children at very different levels, and teachers move on with the syllabus without knowing who understood. In the pilot, one teacher reported planning four lessons a day. A useful support tool must shorten preparation, make learning visible without student devices, and turn results into an actionable next lesson. Saathi is designed as a closed loop rather than a one-off text generator. ASER 2024 reports that 23.4% of Class 3 government-school children could read a Class 2-level text, 27.6% could do two-digit subtraction, 30.7% of Class 5 children could do three-digit by one-digit division, and 44.8% of Class 5 government-school children could read a Class 2-level text (ASER 2024 National Findings, pp. 46–48, https://asercentre.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/ASER-2024-National-findings.pdf). UDISE+ 2024–25 reports 104,125 single-teacher schools enrolling 3,376,769 students, including 5,001 schools and 62,288 students in Telangana (Table 2.2, https://educationforallinindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/single-teacher-zero-enrolment-schools-UDISEPlus-2024-25-DoSEL.pdf). Deccan Chronicle reported a NIEPA study finding government teachers spend 19.1% of working hours teaching; this was reported journalism, not an official publication (22 September 2018, https://deccanchronicle.com/nation/current-affairs/220918/teachers-spend-only-191-per-cent-time-teaching.html).

Evidence rule. The pilot wording is: piloted with real data from three classrooms. The data does not establish causal learning gains or sustained teacher adoption.

2. What is new

ChatGPT and Gemini are broad assistants; MagicSchool AI and Khanmigo offer educator workflows; DIKSHA offers a large content ecosystem; Plickers and Google Forms collect responses. Saathi’s narrower proposition is a curriculum-aware Plan → Check → Next steps loop: teachers print paper checks, children need no device, code computes marks and readiness groups, and the Coach turns those groups into the next lesson.

CapabilitySaathi’s approachTrade-off
Student devicesNone requiredPaper upload/reading remains operational work
DiagnosisCode-derived counts and readiness groupsAnswer-key and sheet-reading errors need review
Next actionCoach plus differentiated resourcesLibrary coverage is still limited

3. The agents and the loop

Plan→Print→Upload→Analyse→Next steps
AgentTool/output
Lesson PlannerTwo-half lesson plan and differentiated method
Check BuilderPrintable answer key and child-facing check
Answer Sheet ReaderTranscription suggestions; code marks against the key
ReviewerMust-fix checks and revision where needed
Next-Step CoachLow/Mid/High group actions
Resource BuilderWorksheet, meeting plan, or leader one-pager

Plain Python handles roll import, marking, mastery/readiness maths, support-child selection, arithmetic checks, name insertion, ownership, and budgets. That keeps deterministic decisions inspectable and prevents an LLM from inventing class statistics.

4. One traced full loop

This is one real run of the whole loop, recorded by scripts/trace_loop.py with the demo account and the committed sample files (no real classroom data). A Grade 3 Telangana class was created with the sample 38-child roll, a five-step place-value lesson was planned, five sample answer sheets were uploaded and read, and the results flowed into Next steps, a worksheet and the next lesson's warm-up.

What each agent did. The Lesson Planner called its tools for the curriculum context, the class profile and the latest insight, then wrote the two-half plan. The Check Builder turned the plan into a five-question answer key. The Reviewer found a must-fix issue, so the planner revised the plan once and the Reviewer checked it again. Five Answer Sheet Reader calls transcribed one sheet each; code then marked the answers against the key and computed the analysis without any model call. The Next-Step Coach wrote the re-teaching plan and warm-up; a second review triggered one Coach revision. The Resource Builder then wrote the three-level worksheets.

6. Safety and privacy

Evidence covers account-level 401 and ownership 404 defenses, lockout, budgets, reset-link safety, prompt-injection handling, numeric Coach checks, reviewer must-fix handling, and safe rendering of model text. The committed safety file should be read alongside this section. Children’s names and answer-sheet images are excluded from this report and repository. The app uses roll numbers and first names in teacher-facing outputs; names are not sent to the model as part of the intended flow.

The safety evidence deliberately distinguishes automated tests from pilot observations. The committed accounts check and pytest output are the reproducible defense records; no claim is made that every injection scenario was exercised during the classroom pilot.

7. Impact

Wording: piloted with real data from three classrooms.

## Verified counts

- Classrooms: 3
- Children: 118
- Sheets: 118
- Answers Read: 590
- Results: 590
- Insights: 3
- Feedback Entries: 4

## Recorded feedback (redacted)

- Ratings recorded: 4; mean: 3.75.
- Saathi minutes recorded: 2.0, 2.0, 3.0, 2.0.
- Teacher names and free-text comments are excluded from the committed export.

Recorded feedback has a mean rating of 3.75 across four entries, with Saathi times of 2, 2, 3, and 2 minutes. The coordinator’s notes record requests for stronger real-life problems, story context, visuals, and more classroom context. These are recorded observations—not proof of learning gains or teacher adoption.

Future impact measurement should use independent baseline and endline assessments, comparison classrooms, and repeated observation. Hours saved should be estimated only after a larger, consistently measured sample.

8. Limits and next steps

  • Bugs seen in the final demo run: the Coach summary counted 25 answers as '25 children' (it was 5 children), and the existing number check did not catch it because 25 appears in the results; one top error was listed twice; the plan's expected-student-response field showed raw structured text; the bottom tab bar can cover content on long pages.
  • Grade 2 readiness results were inverted and need verification.
  • An English/Maths label mix-up and a first Grade 5 plan failure were observed.
  • Uploaded results currently confirm automatically; teacher review before confirmation is still needed.
  • Chapter coverage, other-subject misconception libraries, offline mode, photo/QR capture, WhatsApp practice, and persistent production hosting remain future work.

Next: verify chapter data for both boards, expand EVS and English support, add offline capture, and run a proper comparison-class pilot.

Appendix A. The three-classroom pilot

The pilot dataset was filtered by the three pilot teacher accounts, excluding the demo teacher and its classes. It contains three classroom papers, 118 children, 118 uploaded sheets, and 590 answer records. The three classes were Grade 2A Telangana with 38 children, Grade 4B NCERT with 37 children, and Grade 5A Telangana with 43 children. These counts reconcile exactly: 38 + 37 + 43 = 118; five answers per sheet produce 590 answers.

ClassBoard / subjectChildrenTopic and methodPlan timeAverageLow / Mid / High
Grade 2ATelangana · Maths38One-digit addition with carry over · 5-step · Process26s29.5%40% / 26.3% / 25%
Grade 4BNCERT · English37The Sounds of Bells · 5-step · Process + Product31s81.1%51.1% / 80% / 97.6%
Grade 5ATelangana · Maths43Everyday measurement problems · 5E · Content + Product54s successful62.8%38.8% / 71.1% / 88.9%

The Grade 2 result is intentionally shown rather than averaged away. Low readiness scoring above Mid and High is an inverted pattern. It may reflect an answer-key problem, assessment difficulty, grouping error, or sheet-reading issue; it is not evidence that the readiness model is correct. The Grade 4 and Grade 5 patterns are more conventional, but still require checking against actual work.

Planning time was 26–54 seconds for the selected successful plans. Grade 5 had an initial failure after 24 seconds with a misleading API-key message; retries and clearer failure handling allowed the later 54-second run. The recorded full-workflow costs in the coordinator notes were approximately $0.010–$0.021 per classroom. The database token ledger is the authoritative source for the detailed model costs in the Tokenomics section.

Appendix B. Pilot feedback and interpretation

Four feedback entries were recorded across the three accounts. Ratings were 3, 3, 4, and 5, with a mean of 3.75. The reported Saathi times were two, two, three, and two minutes. Usual planning-time categories ranged from under 15 minutes to over 60 minutes, so the baseline is inconsistent and should not be converted into a precise hours-saved claim.

The feedback comments are the teachers' own words. For example, Anurag wrote, ‘I like how the platform provides an integrated differentiation option that's a blessing for a beginner teacher like me... I need to plan 4 lessons everyday and I can do them now in 30 minutes...’ Janhavi wrote, ‘I would like to see if the AI can pull context of the story to desgin the assignment than keeping it general... maybe can add pictures given grade 4 children learn visuals.’ Anjali wrote, ‘I would like to make the assignment more rigorous and bring questions around real life.’ The spelling and punctuation are preserved from pilot.db. The Grade 2 feedback requested more rigorous real-life word problems and differentiation inside assignments. The Grade 4 feedback requested story-specific questions and pictures appropriate for Grade 4. The Grade 5 feedback valued differentiation, checking progress, and planning the next class, while also requesting more classroom context. One observation was that a teacher plans four lessons a day and reported completing them in 30 minutes; this is a single recorded observation, not a population estimate.

The strongest interpretation is operational: the app can produce a structured plan quickly and connect a paper assessment to suggested next actions. The weakest interpretation would be that it improved learning or will save every teacher a fixed amount of time. The pilot cannot support that claim. A proper follow-up would collect pre-specified planning times, observe edits, compare independent baseline/endline assessments, and include comparison classrooms.

Privacy choice: no children's names, teacher names, free-text comments, or answer-sheet images are included in the committed evidence export. The redacted CSV preserves feedback ratings, decisions, time categories, and timing fields only.

Appendix C. Implementation and measurement detail

The interface is intentionally split into a teacher-facing sequence and a code-owned measurement layer. The teacher chooses class context, subject, chapter, topic, lesson type, and optional differentiation. The Lesson Planner produces the lesson vision and method. The Check Builder turns the lesson into an answer key. The teacher prints the check and uploads completed sheets. The Answer Sheet Reader supplies transcription suggestions, while ordinary Python matches roll numbers, applies the answer key, calculates marks, and groups children by readiness. The insight then becomes the input to the Coach and resource builders.

This division matters because the model should not be trusted to add a child to a group, calculate a percentage, or silently repair an answer key. The code can show exactly which result led to a Low, Mid, or High grouping. Model output is treated as untrusted text: it is validated, reviewed where appropriate, and escaped before rendering. Teacher text is also untrusted and is screened for prompt-injection patterns. Budgets and ownership checks are enforced at the API boundary.

The app currently confirms uploaded results automatically after reading and marking. That is the accurate behavior in this build. It is not accurate to describe the workflow as waiting for a teacher to confirm a grid. Teacher review before confirmation is therefore a clear next product step, alongside better answer-key checks. The pilot's Grade 2 inversion and Grade 5 initial failure show why that review matters.

The database also records model calls, cached input, output tokens, provider cost, application cost, and duration. The aggregate evidence uses those rows, filtered to the three pilot teacher IDs. It does not mix demo activity into pilot numbers. A future full-loop trace should join runs, LLM calls, tool calls, review results, and screenshots by run ID; the present report only claims fields that are present in the committed evidence.

Evidence gallery

These demo-fixture screenshots show the states discussed above; they contain no real classroom data.

Trace reading. The planner received the Grade 3 Telangana class, Mathematics, Place value, and a five-step lesson request. It called curriculum context, class profile, and latest-insight tools before producing the two-half plan. The reviewer then checked the plan; the first output was revised once by the planner, which is why the trace contains both the original and revision calls. The Check Builder received the plan and called the misconception tool to create the answer key. The revised plan and check were retained in the temporary database used for this run.

The reader handled five fixture sheets. Each call received the sheet image plus the instruction to read the roll number and answers; the deterministic layer then matched each answer against the key. The trace reports five reader calls rather than hiding them inside a batch total. After confirmation, the analysis endpoint used stored results, question keys, and readiness levels; no second model diagnosis was needed. The Coach received the code-owned insight, called class-profile and misconception tools, and was revised once after review. Finally, the Resource Builder received the same insight and produced the worksheet. This is the key architectural boundary: models suggest language and activities, while code owns counts, percentages, grouping, and confirmation state.
